B.explanation: Deriving $R=V/I$ to base units gives $\text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-3}\text{ A}^{-2}$, which matches this option.

C.explanation: This is $\text{kg m s}^{-2}\text{ A}^{-1}$, which is the unit of force divided by current, not voltage divided by current.

hints: Start from resistance in ohms as $R = V/I$, so you need the SI base units of voltage divided by the base unit of current $\text{A}$.
Write voltage as energy per charge, $V = W/Q$, where work $W$ is in $\text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$ and charge $Q$ is in $\text{A s}$.
Combine to get $V$ in base units, then divide once more by $\text{A}$ for $R = V/I$ and check the powers of $\text{m}$, $\text{s}$ and $\text{A}$.
walkthrough: Recall $R = V/I$, so $1$ ohm $= 1$ volt per ampere. The base unit for current $I$ is $\text{A}$.
Write potential difference as $V = W/Q$, energy transferred per unit charge. Energy $W$ has unit joule $= \text{N m} = \text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$.
Charge $Q = It$ has unit coulomb $= \text{A s}$. So $V$ in base units is $\dfrac{\text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}}{\text{A s}} = \text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-3}\text{ A}^{-1}$.
Now divide by current for resistance: $R = V/I$ gives $\dfrac{\text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-3}\text{ A}^{-1}}{\text{A}} = \text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-3}\text{ A}^{-2}$.
